Consider convexity. A circle is convex all throughout the perimeter, so any cut it makes is convex for half of the cut (the part closer to the circle's center) and is concave for the other part. We start off with a single circle which is convex. Take that as the base case. Now assume by induction we have a piece that is completely convex. A extra cut through that piece can separate it into 2 pieces, a piece with a hole through it or 3 pieces. If it is 2 pieces, it is easy to see that the piece closer to the center has a convex side added, which means the shape is purely convex. If there is a piece with a hole, the "hole" itself as a circle is purely convex. If 3 pieces are created, the middle piece has 2 extra convex sides, which maintains the purely-convexity. So by induction there exists a piece that is purely convex.

Next we can prove that there also exists a concave shape. There are at least 2 black pieces, so there must be at least one cut of a circle through a circle which creates at least one concave piece. Then, no number of convex cuts can make the concave arc "no longer concave". So the concave arc always exists, meaning there is always a concave shape.

A concave shape is definitely not congruent to a convex shape, so it is impossible for all pieces to be congruent.
